Foundations of Data Collection

  • Data collection: Gathering raw data from different sources.
  • High-quality data is essential for analysis, AI, and decision-making.
  • Examples:
    • Many polls leading up to the election incorrectly predicted a Hillary Clinton victory. Several factors contributed, but flawed data collection was a key issue.
    • manufacturing company deploys thousands of IoT sensors to monitor equipment performance. These sensors generate massive volumes of time-series data, exceeding the capacity of their existing data ingestion pipeline.

Data Sources

  • Structured Data
    • Data organized in a predefined format, typically with rows and columns, making it easily searchable and analyzable.
  • Semi-structured Data
    • Data that has some internal organization but doesn't adhere to a strict format like tables. It often uses tags or markers to identify elements.
  • Unstructured Data
    • Data that lacks a predefined format or organization.

Data Sources: Structured

  • Structured data: organized in a predefined format, typically with rows and columns, making it easily searchable and analyzable
  • Examples:
    • Databases: Relational: MySQL, PostgreSQL and NoSQL: MongoDB, Cassandra
    • APIs (Application Programming Interfaces that provide structured data)
    • CSVs
  • Benefits:
    • Easily understood by machines
    • Ideal for traditional data analysis
    • Requires less storage
  • Drawbacks:
    • Limited representations

Data Sources: Semi-structured

  • Semi-structured data: has some internal organization but doesn't adhere to a strict format like tables, often uses tags or markers to identify elements
  • Examples:
    • Logs (Server logs, application logs, event logs)
    • XML (Extensible Markup Language)
    • JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)
    • NoSQL databases
    • IoT sensor data (can also be unstructured if device send out raw data,like raw audio, images/video, binary sensor dumps,…)*
  • Benefits:
    • More flexibility
    • Can represent more complex relationships than structured data
  • Drawbacks:
    • Requires parsing or schema definition for analysis

* IoT text/numeric streams = semi-structured , IoT audio/video = unstructured

Data Sources: Unstructured

  • Unstructured data: Data that lacks a predefined format or organization
  • Examples:
    • Images
    • Videos
    • Text
    • Social media posts
  • Benefits:
    • Contains rich information
  • Drawbacks:
    • requires specialized techniques for analysis, such as natural language processing (NLP), image recognition, or video analysis
    • Requires more storage

Quick exercise: Identify the Data Type

  • IoT temperature stream
    • Timestamp, Temperature value
      • Semi-structured -> often JSON or device-specific schema, time-series with flexible format
  • Bank transactions
    • Amount, date, card ID, category, …
      • Structured -> fixed fields, rows/columns
  • Instagram story
    • Image + text overlay + metadata
      • Unstructured -> images + free text
      • But the metadata (timestamp, user_id, geolocation) = structured
  • Response fromGithubAPI
    • User info, repos, links
      • Semi-structured-> format of responses toAPI are : JSON, XML or tekst (in thiscase JSON)

Practical Data Collection Techniques

  • Web scraping: automated extraction of data from websites
  • APIs: data access from web services
  • Database queries: retrieving data from databases
  • Data streaming: capturing data from ‘live’ sources
  • Sensor-Based Collection: IoT devices, logs, monitoring systems

Data Collection: Web Scraping

  • Tools:
    • Beautiful Soup: python library for parsing HTML and XML
    • Scrapy: python framework for building web scrapers
  • Considerations:
    • Legal and ethical: respect website terms of service and robot instructions
    • Website structure: understanding HTML and CSS
    • Rate limiting: avoid overloading the server

Data Collection: APIs

An API (Application Programming Interface) allows applications to communicate with each other by exposing specific data or functionality.

Whyis itused:

    • structured and predictable way to request data
    • Safer thanscraping
    • Widely used in modern data platforms

Real worldexamples:

    • GitHub API → repositorydata
    • OpenWeatherAPI → weatherdata
    • SpotifyAPI → musicmetadata

Componentsof anAPI Request

  • Endpoint: The URL where the data lives.
    • https://api.example.com/users
  • Method: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
    • Data engineers mainly use GET for collection
  • Parameters: Modify or filter the request.
    • ?limit=10&sort=desc
  • Headers: Authentication, format specifications.

API AuthenticationTypes

API RateLimits& Pagination

Rate Limits: APIs restrict how many requests per minute/hour you can send.

    • Preventsoverloadingservers
    • Ingestionpipelinesmust obeylimits

Pagination: APIs return data in pages. For example, GitHub returns 30 items per page. Youringestionmust:

    • track next page URL
    • loop until all items are collected

Data Collection: Databases

  • Tools:
    • SQL clients
    • sqlite3 or psycopg2: python libraries with sql integration
    • GraphQL: query language for APIs to request specific data
  • Considerations:
    • Database schema: data structure
    • Optimization: efficient queries
    • Data security: protect sensitive data
    • GDPR: limits how we use data

Data Collection: Streaming

  • Tools:
    • Kafka: distributed streaming platform for handling high-volume data streams
    • Flink: data stream processing framework
  • Considerations:
    • Data velocity and volume: high-speed,continuous data
    • Latency: aim for minimal delays
    • Infrastructure: scalable and reliable

Data Collection: IoT

  • Types of IoT Data
    • Equipment data: Status and performance of machines or devices
    • Environmental Data: information on temperature, humidity, etc.
  • Tools
    • HTTP/HTTPS: Standard web protocols for data transmission
    • Edge Computing: Processing data near the source to reduce latency
  • Considerations
    • Data security: Ensuring the protection of collected data
    • Data privacy: Protecting user data and complying with regulations
    • Data management: Handling large volumes of data efficiently
    • Interoperability: Ensuring different devices and systems work together seamlessly
    • Scalability: Managing the growing number of connected devices and data volume

Data Ingestion Fundamentals

  • Data Ingestion: The process of importing, transferring, and preparing raw data for analysis or storage in a target system (e.g., data warehouse, data lake, database).
  • Goals:
    • Efficient Data Flow: ensures smooth and automated movement of data from various sources to your analytics systems
    • Data Transformation: prepares data for analysis by cleaning, transforming, and structuring it
    • Data Availability: makes data readily accessible for analysis, reporting, and decision-making
    • Scalability: handles increasing data volumes and velocities as your needs grow.
  • Example: Netflix ingests real-time user activity data to improve recommendations

Data Ingestion Process

Data Ingestion Process

Batch vs. Real-Time Ingestion

  • Data ingestion can be processed in a batch (like a mail delivery once a day) or in real-time (like a continuous conveyor belt).

Batch Ingestion

  • Batch Processing: ingestingdata in scheduledbatches, e.g., hourly, daily
  • Examples:
    • ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) jobs fordata warehousing, SQL importsforloadingdata intodatabases, processing log files collectedover a period
  • UseCases:
    • Generating dailyor weeklyreports, historicaldata analysis, data migrations
  • Benefits:
    • Simplerto implement, efficientforlarge data volumes, cost-effectiveforlesstime-sensitivedata.
  • Drawbacks:
    • Higherlatency(data is notavailable immediately)

Real-time Ingestion

  • Real-time Processing: ingesting data continuously as it's generated, minimal delay
  • Examples:
    • Streaming data fromIoTdevices, pocessingsocialmedia feeds, analyzingfinancial transactions.
  • UseCases:
    • Fraud detection, real-time dashboards and monitoring, personalized recommendations
  • Benefits:
    • Immediateinsights, enablesreal-time actions andresponses, supports event-drivenarchitectures
  • Drawbacks:
    • More complex to implement,requiresspecializedtools andinfrastructure, canbemoreexpensive

Comparing Batch and Real-time

  • This is a key distinction in data ingestion: batch vs real-time
  • Choosing the Right Approach:
    • Data Velocity: How fast is the data generated?
    • Latency Requirements: How quickly do you need insights?
    • Context: What are you trying to achieve with the data?

Ingestion Challenges

Data rarely arrives clean, consistent or complete

Some common pain points:

    • Schema drift
    • System failures
    • Corruptedrecords
    • Duplicatedata
    • Time zone inconsistencies

Challenge: Schema drift

Schema drift = unexpected changes in data format

Examples:

    • New column appears
    • field suddenlybecomesnull
    • JSON object addsnesteddata

Pipelines maybreak becauseof schema drift

Challenge: Data Quality Issues

Examples:

    • Missing values
    • Incorrect types
    • Unusualspikes
    • Wrong timestamps

-> Validateyourdata at ingestionstage

Challenge: Handling Errors & Retries

Pipeline must handle:

    • Network outages
    • API timeouts
    • Partial failures

Best practices:

    • Retry with backoff
    • Log failures
    • Store bad records separatelyalsocalled‘dead-letter queue’

Challenge: Ordering & Timestamps

Incoming data may be:

    • Out of order
    • Duplicated
    • Delayed

Neededfor:

    • Correct aggregations
    • Accurate time-series
    • Detectinglate-arrivingdata

Data Ingestion Architectures

Direct Ingestion Architecture (1)

Direct ingestion is the simplest form of moving data from a source into a storage system (data lake, warehouse, database) without an intermediary system like Kafka or Spark.You pull or receive data directly from the source.

  • API-basedIngestion
    • Pulling data from REST/GraphQL APIs
    • Frequently used for SaaS tools (HubSpot, GitHub, Stripe, Google Analytics)
    • Data arrives as JSON or XML
    • Often scheduled at intervals (e.g., every 10 minutes)
  • File Uploads
    • Manually uploaded CSV, Excel, JSON files
    • Automated file drops in S3, Azure Blob, Google Cloud Storage
    • “Landing zone” approach (data engineers watch a storage folder for new files)
  • Database Imports
    • Direct SQL queries
    • Export/import tools

Direct Ingestion Architecture (2)

Strengths

    • Easy toset up
    • Low cost
    • Ideal for small/medium data volumes
    • Good for periodic data collection (batch pulls)

Weaknesses

    • Not suitable for high-volume or real-time data
    • Harder toscale
    • Source system canbecomeoverloaded
    • decoupling → if the source is down, ingestion stops

UseCases

    • Pulling weather data from an API
    • Loading CSVs from partners or students
    • Syncing product lists or HR exports
    • Collecting small external datasets for analytics

Streaming Processing Architecture (1)

What is it

    • Streaming ingestion processes data continuously, in real time, as events occur.
    • Instead of waiting for a batch, each event is delivered immediately:
    • user clicks on a page
    • sensor sendstemperature
    • customer performsa transaction
    • Each one generates an event that flows into a streaming system.

Kafka

    • Distributed event log
    • High throughput& faulttolerance
    • UsedbyNetflix, Uber, Spotify

SparkStreaming

    • Processesmicro-batches
    • Often used for real-time transformation

Flink

    • True real-time (no micro-batches)
    • Great forcomplex event processing

Batch Pipeline Architecture (1)

What It Is

    • Batch ingestion collects data in bulk at regular intervals, not continuously:
      • nceper hour
      • nceper day
      • every5 minutes
    • Instead of event-by-event, you ingest a whole dataset in one go.

Apache Airflow

    • Orchestratesmulti-step pipelines
    • Used widely in modern data engineering
    • Scheduler+ dependencymanager

Cloud ManagedPipelines

    • AWS GlueJobs
    • AzureData Factory

Strengths

    • Easy toreasonabout

    • Fewersystem requirementsthanstreaming

Weaknesses

Data Ingestion: ETL vs ELT

  • ETL: Extract, Transform, Load
  • ELT: Extract, Load, Transform
  • When and where datatransformation occurs has an impact on:
    • Efficiency
    • Flexibility
    • Tool choice

Consider: data volume, velocity, variety, and context.

Data Storage: Data Warehouse

  • Centralized storage optimized for structured, relational data.
  • Key Features:
    • Schema-on-write (data modeled before loading).
    • Optimized for SQL queries, reporting, and BI.
  • Examples: Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery, Snowflake.
  • Pros: High performance, consistent data, governance.
  • Cons: Less flexible with unstructured data, higher upfront modeling effort.

Data Storage: Data Lake

  • Central repository for raw, semi-structured, and unstructured data.
  • Key Features:
    • Schema-on-read (data structured only when accessed).
    • Supports large volumes & diverse formats (CSV, JSON, Parquet, images, logs).
  • Examples: AWS S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, GCP Cloud Storage
  • Use Cases: Machine learning, exploratory analytics, IoT data, logs.
  • Pros: Flexible, scalable, cost-efficient.
  • Cons: Risk of “data swamp” without governance.

Data Storage: Data Lakehouses

  • Hybrid architecture combining best of data lakes + warehouses.
  • Key Features:
    • Stores all data types (structured & unstructured).
    • Supports both BI queries and AI/ML workloads.
    • ACID transactions and governance built-in.
  • Examples: Databricks Delta Lake, Snowflake, Google BigLake.
  • Benefits: Unified storage, flexibility, reduced data duplication.
  • Challenges: Complexity, vendor lock-in, evolving ecosystem.

Data Ingestion Considerations

Data Governance & Metadata in Ingestion

  • Governance Goals: Ensure data quality, compliance, and security.
  • Key Elements:
    • Data Quality: Validation, deduplication, consistency checks.
    • Metadata Management: Catalogs for lineage & discoverability.
    • Security & Privacy: Access control, encryption, GDPR/HIPAA compliance.
    • Observability: Monitoring pipelines, error tracking, performance logging.
  • Without Governance: Risk of bad data, compliance violations, and loss of trust in analytics.
  • “Garbage in, garbage out” principle

What is the difference between Data Collection and Data ingestion?

  • Scope: Data collection is about gathering data, while data ingestion is about moving and preparing that data for use.
  • Process: Data collection involves capturing raw data, whereas data ingestion involves transforming and integrating that data into a system.
  • Outcome: The result of data collection is raw data, while the result of data ingestion is data that is ready for analysis and decision-making

Conclusion: Data collection and ingestion form the foundation of every data-driven system.
